## Foundations: Empirical Power Laws in Deep Learning and Language Models

The idea that neural network performance improves predictably with scale has strong empirical support from before large language models. Across machine translation, language modelling, image classification and speech recognition, Hestness et al. found that generalization error falls as a power law of training-set size, and that the model size needed to fit the data also grows as a power law of data size [hestness2017]. The exponent depended mainly on the task domain and was less sensitive to model architecture. Learning curves showed three regions: a small-data region, a power-law region, and an irreducible-error region [hestness2017].

Kaplan et al. extended this to neural language models. They showed that cross-entropy loss follows smooth power laws in non-embedding parameters, dataset size and training compute over more than seven orders of magnitude, provided the other two factors are not a bottleneck [kaplan2020]. Within a wide range, architectural details such as depth versus width mattered little. Larger models were more sample-efficient, reaching the same loss with fewer tokens. For a fixed compute budget, the paper recommended growing model size faster than dataset size and stopping training before convergence [kaplan2020].

The GPT-4 Technical Report offered practical validation of these regularities. GPT-4's final training loss was predicted in advance from much smaller runs, using up to 1,000 to 10,000 times less compute, by fitting a power law [openai2023]. Pass rate on a subset of HumanEval was also forecast this way. However, not every capability was predictable, and some tasks showed unexpected trends [openai2023].

---

## Compute-Optimal Training: Chinchilla and Data Constraints

Early scaling-law work found that language-model loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute, provided the other two are not a bottleneck [kaplan2020]. Because larger models proved more sample-efficient, that analysis recommended that, for a fixed compute budget, model size should grow faster than dataset size and training should stop before convergence [kaplan2020].

Chinchilla revised this picture. Hoffmann et al. found that, for a fixed budget, parameters and training tokens should be scaled in roughly equal proportion, which gives a rule of thumb of about 20 tokens per parameter [hoffmann2022]. On this view, many large models of the time, including Gopher and GPT-3, were undertrained for their size. Chinchilla itself, with 70B parameters trained on about 1.4 trillion tokens, outperformed the 280B-parameter Gopher trained with the same compute [hoffmann2022].

Scaling data alongside parameters raises a practical question: what happens when unique text runs out? Muennighoff et al. found that repetition helps up to a point. Training for up to about four epochs on repeated data is nearly as good as using unique data [muennighoff2023]. Beyond that, the value of additional repeated tokens decays towards zero, and with many more repetitions, adding compute stops helping [muennighoff2023]. To stretch a limited text budget, they point to mixing in code data or relaxing quality filters as practical strategies [muennighoff2023].

---

## Beyond Training Compute: Inference-Aware and Test-Time Scaling

The Chinchilla analysis set the reference point for compute-optimal training. For a fixed training budget, parameters and training tokens should grow in roughly equal proportion, which gives a rule of thumb of about 20 tokens per parameter [hoffmann2022]. Chinchilla (70B parameters, about 1.4T tokens) outperformed the 280B-parameter Gopher trained with the same compute [hoffmann2022]. However, this analysis optimizes training compute only.

Sardana and Frankle extend the objective to the model's total lifetime cost, which includes both training and inference compute [sardana2023]. When expected inference demand is high, total cost is lower if a smaller model is trained on more tokens than the Chinchilla ratio suggests. This helps explain why recent models are often trained far past 20 tokens per parameter [sardana2023].

A second line of work treats inference compute as a scaling axis in its own right, alongside parameters and training data [snell2024]. Extra compute can be spent on sequential revisions or on verifier-guided search. Allocating it adaptively by question difficulty was more than four times more efficient than a best-of-N baseline [snell2024]. On easier and medium-difficulty questions, a smaller model given additional test-time compute could beat a much larger model. On the hardest questions, however, scaling pretraining remained more effective [snell2024].

Taken together, these results suggest that compute allocation should consider training, serving and per-query reasoning jointly rather than training alone. Smaller, longer-trained models can lower serving costs [sardana2023]. Test-time compute can partly substitute for parameters, though this substitution has limits on the most difficult problems [snell2024].

---

## Emergent Abilities and the Limits of Predictability

Training loss falls smoothly with scale, but it does not follow that downstream capabilities do. [wei2022] call an ability emergent if it is absent in smaller models but present in larger ones. They argue such abilities cannot be predicted by simply extrapolating from smaller scales. Their examples include multi-step arithmetic under few-shot prompting and the gains from chain-of-thought prompting. They report that prompting techniques like chain-of-thought only help beyond a certain model scale [wei2022].

[schaeffer2023] contest this reading, arguing that apparent emergence is often produced by the choice of metric. All-or-nothing measures such as exact-match accuracy can turn smooth underlying improvement into a sudden jump. When the same outputs are scored with continuous metrics such as token edit distance, performance improves smoothly and predictably [schaeffer2023]. They recommend checking emergence claims against the metric used and the number of models evaluated [schaeffer2023].

The debate matters for forecasting capabilities before training. The GPT-4 report describes infrastructure built to scale predictably. GPT-4's final loss was predicted with a fitted power law from runs using 1,000 to 10,000 times less compute [openai2023]. Its pass rate on a subset of HumanEval was forecast in advance in the same way [openai2023]. The report also acknowledges that not every capability was predictable, since some tasks showed unexpected trends [openai2023]. Together, these findings suggest that forecasting is feasible for some metrics. Whether a capability looks predictable may depend heavily on how it is measured.

---

- [kaplan2020] Kaplan et al. (OpenAI) (2020). Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
- [muennighoff2023] Muennighoff et al. (2023). Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
- [openai2023] OpenAI (2023). GPT-4 Technical Report
- [sardana2023] Sardana and Frankle (2023). Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws
- [schaeffer2023] Schaeffer, Miranda, Koyejo (2023). Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
- [snell2024] Snell et al. (2024). Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
- [wei2022] Wei et al. (2022). Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
